title: First Weeks #2: What Are My Priorities in the Classroom? he-classroom/
author: Peter Foster
summary: In the second post of a series aimed at new teachers, Peter Foster lays out how to establish behaviour and work expectations in the first lessons of a school year. On behaviour, he recommends leaning on existing school policy rather than inventing expectations from scratch, using naturally-occurring 'teachable moments' to demonstrate expectations rather than relying solely on an opening speech, and scripting and rehearsing the specific phrases used for recurring instructions so language stays consistent and doesn't drift under pressure. On work expectations, he argues teachers rarely make participation expectations explicit the way they do behaviour expectations, and recommends stating clearly upfront that every student will be involved in every lesson, then following through with practised routines (talk partners, mini-whiteboards) and consistent checking that every student answers a question regularly, not just the volunteers. He closes with the advice to keep holding these standards even when a class seems to be going well or when the teacher is tired, since letting up, even subconsciously, gets noticed and adjusted to by students.
points: Foster recommends demonstrating behaviour expectations through real-time 'teachable moments' rather than relying only on an opening-day speech, arguing show-don't-tell works better than a one-off lecture.

He advises scripting and rehearsing the exact phrases used for recurring instructions, arguing consistent language both helps students learn routines faster and prevents teachers from becoming vaguer under pressure.

He argues teachers routinely state behaviour expectations explicitly but rarely do the same for participation expectations, and recommends stating upfront that every student will be involved every lesson.

His closing advice, to keep standards up even when a class seems to be going well or the teacher is tired, is framed as a warning that any perceptible let-up will be noticed and exploited by students, even subconsciously.
quotes: I’d summarise your aim in the first week’s lessons like this: establish your expectations of student behaviour and expectations of student work in your classroom.

Instead of, or in addition to, having this talk about your expectations at the start of the year, look out for moments to demonstrate your expectations to the class. Show, don’t tell, as much as possible.
For instructions that will repeat, there’s merit to using the same language each time we share them.
I’ve seen lots of teachers introduce their expectations of student behaviour but I’ve rarely seen teachers introduce their expectation of student work.
If we want all the children to participate in every lesson, we want to make sure they're ready for it. You can practise just about every routine or act in the classroom.
If we let up on that expectation, students will notice and, perhaps subconsciously, adjust their behaviour.
